section_summary: The section finishes a translation of regulations under Japan’s Automobile Manufacturing Industry Law, then begins a June 1936 Yokohama consular report on the Japanese automotive industry. The report examines demand, production costs, military purchasing, American assembly plants, roads, and government support. Its enclosures include interview memoranda, tariff and production figures, legal excerpts, and press reports.

subfiles.title: Enforcing regulations for the Automobile Manufacturing Industry Law, concluding pages
subfiles.about: Application, reporting, and approval rules for automobile manufacturers and duty-free imports.
subfiles.summary: Articles 9–30 prescribe applications and reports concerning imported goods, financing, annual plans, transfers, mergers, dissolution, and production. Transitional rules address existing manufacturers. An annex lists materials, instruments, and machinery eligible under the regulations.

subfiles.title: Submission of report on the Japanese automotive industry
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Transmits a report prepared by Boyce and Vice Consul Merrill.
subfiles.summary: Boyce submits the collaborative report and a list of earlier reports.

subfiles.title: Japanese Automotive Industry
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce and Gregor C. Merrill, American Consulate, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Assesses Japan’s automobile industry, markets, costs, quality, and government support.
subfiles.summary: The report argues that defense policy and national pride, rather than ordinary market demand, drive the effort to establish a domestic industry. It surveys small civilian markets, Datsun and truck production, exports, military demand, labor, materials, machinery, design, roads, and gasoline costs. The authors conclude that limited scale and high costs make Japanese producers dependent on subsidies and protective rules, while American assembly plants face prospective quotas and tariffs.

subfiles.title: Visa memorandum concerning two Nissan engineers
subfiles.about: Records visas for Nissan engineers visiting the Graham-Paige plant.
subfiles.summary: Hatamura and Harashina plan to study production methods and test a new motor in Detroit.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Thomas Belsjoe of Chrysler Corporation
subfiles.about: Discusses automobile quotas and barriers to Japanese competition with American cars.
subfiles.summary: Belsjoe describes prospective quotas and higher tariffs, then attributes Japan’s weak competitive position to imported materials, limited production scale, and delayed access to American designs. He also discusses labor, patents, and locally made replacement parts.

subfiles.title: Conversation with S. Yamamoto of Nissan
subfiles.about: Records Nissan’s account of Datsun sales and plans for a larger car.
subfiles.summary: Yamamoto describes Datsun production, sales, vehicle life, and the abandonment of exports. He outlines plans to buy machinery abroad and produce a larger car at a price below American competitors. He also discusses expected market growth, quotas, labor, and road building.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Thomas Belsjoe of Chrysler Export Corporation
subfiles.about: Discusses industrial self-sufficiency, Toyoda subsidies, Nissan machinery, and diesel trucks.
subfiles.summary: Belsjoe predicts automobile quotas and describes the military aim of independent truck production. He estimates Toyoda’s reliance on subsidies and explains Chrysler’s response to the policy. He reports that Nissan sought machinery from Graham-Paige and doubts Mitsubishi diesel trucks would compete effectively.

subfiles.title: Duties and Freight Rates as of June 1, 1936
subfiles.about: Lists import duties and freight rates for automobiles, parts, steel, and machinery.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure gives tariff classifications and rates for cars, parts, alloy steel, and machine tools. It also lists shipping rates from Atlantic and Pacific ports and estimates freight costs for cars and heavy machinery.

subfiles.title: Excerpts from the New Law for the Advancement of Automobile Industry in Japan
subfiles.about: Summarizes ownership, tax, tariff, permit, and existing-producer provisions.
subfiles.summary: Excerpts outline Japanese ownership rules, exemptions, possible added duties, penalties, and treatment of existing manufacturers.

subfiles.title: Automobile census, production, and export statistics
subfiles.from: Bureau of National Resources and Department of Finance, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Compiles automobile counts, Japanese production, and exports by year and destination.
subfiles.summary: The tables give an October 1935 vehicle census, annual production figures for 1929–1934, and export totals and destinations. They identify the exported vehicles as likely Datsuns.

subfiles.title: Press Excerpts: Enclosures 8, 9 and 10
subfiles.summary: Divider sheet introducing press excerpts numbered 8 through 10.

subfiles.title: Auto Industry Bill: Government To Have Full Control Of Makers
subfiles.from: The Japan Chronicle, Weekly Commercial Supplement
subfiles.about: Reports proposed government controls and incentives for Japanese automobile makers.
subfiles.summary: The article describes a bill requiring manufacturing permits, majority Japanese ownership, and official oversight. It outlines tax relief, facilities for financing, import restrictions, and transitional rights for existing manufacturers.

subfiles.title: Gasoline Price Increase: Five Sen Rise Permitted By Commerce Department
subfiles.from: The Japan Chronicle, Weekly Commercial Supplement
subfiles.about: Reports approval of a five-sen gasoline price increase and taxi operators’ opposition.
subfiles.summary: Gasoline rises to 51 sen per gallon; taxi operators organize against the increase.
